title: Georgia Moped Laws: Who Can Ride, What You Need, and What Happens After a Crash
excerpt: Georgia lets you ride a moped at 15 or older with a license of any class, requires headgear on every operator and passenger at any age, and exempts the moped from registration. Here is what each Code section says, and what a moped crash claim looks like in Georgia.
content:
Georgia moped laws let you ride at 15 or older with a license, instruction permit or limited permit of any class; exempts the moped from registration; and requires headgear on every operator and passenger, at any age — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-351, § 40-2-20(b)(6), § 40-6-352. The registration statute says nothing about insurance.

What counts as a moped in Georgia

The definition is a list, and a machine has to satisfy all of it. Under O.C.G.A. § 40-1-1(28), a Georgia moped is a motor driven cycle with two or three wheels, no more than two brake horsepower, a combustion engine of 50 cubic centimeters or less, a top speed of 30 miles per hour or less on a level road under engine power alone, and an automatic drive system.

Miss one limit and the machine leaves the category: § 40-1-1(30) puts every moped, and every motorcycle of five brake horsepower or less, in the "motor driven cycle" class, and above that the motorcycle rules take over — including the universal helmet requirement in our Georgia helmet laws guide. Machines running under other sections are covered on our e-bike accident claims, electric scooter accident claims and bicycle accident claims pages.

According to the Georgia Governor's Office of Highway Safety's 2024 motorcycle fact sheet, which counts mopeds and motor scooters within its motorcyclist figures, 182 motorcyclists died in Georgia traffic crashes in 2024 (published September 2026).

License, helmet and registration: what Georgia requires

The license. Any class of license, instruction permit or limited permit satisfies O.C.G.A. § 40-6-351, which names no motorcycle endorsement, and the same section sets a floor of 15 years old.

The helmet. Every operator and passenger wears headgear meeting the Commissioner of Public Safety's standards, at any age, under § 40-6-352; approved motorcycle helmets comply.

According to the U.S. Government Publishing Office's text of 49 C.F.R. § 571.218, Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 218 sets minimum performance requirements for helmets designed for use by motorcyclists — the standard behind the DOT label (2023 edition, read September 19, 2026).

Registration and insurance. Georgia exempts mopeds from registration under O.C.G.A. § 40-2-20(b)(6). That section says nothing about insurance, and this page states no rule either way; put the insurance question to a Georgia attorney.

Six Code sections carry the rule set, stated below as the Code states them.

According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety's state-by-state fatality figures, 1,403 people died in Georgia traffic crashes in 2024, a rate of 1.15 per 100 million vehicle miles traveled.

After a moped crash in Georgia

A moped crash is a negligence claim. You pursue the driver who caused it and prove duty, breach, causation and damages, inside two boundaries: you recover if you are less than 50% at fault, with your award cut by your share (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and you generally have two years to sue (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).

Helmet and license points belong to the adjuster, and they are arguments rather than rules: § 40-6-352 states a traffic duty and says nothing about evidence or damages. Our Georgia comparative negligence guide covers the 50% bar; our Georgia filing deadline guide covers the clock.

Eric Roden, Roden Law's founding partner, points out that a moped rider's percentage of fault is decided on the crash evidence — scene photographs, vehicle damage, the treating physicians' findings — and that a case documented in the first weeks leaves that argument little room to operate.

According to the Georgia Governor's Office of Highway Safety's helmet findings in the same fact sheet, riders wearing no helmet were 2.0 times more likely to suffer a fatal injury, and 76% helmet use saved an estimated 92 lives in 2024 — why our traumatic brain injury claims and motorcycle accident claims pages turn on early proof.

How Georgia's rule differs across the state line

South Carolina requires a helmet only for moped riders under 21 and requires the moped itself to be registered, so an adult covered by Georgia's headgear rule rides under a different rule there — our South Carolina moped laws guide covers it, and publishes shortly. Everything above is Georgia law.

meta._roden_key_takeaways: Anyone 15 or older with a license or permit of any class may ride — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-351. Every operator and passenger wears approved headgear at any age — § 40-6-352. Georgia exempts mopeds from registration — § 40-2-20(b)(6), which says nothing about insurance. A moped has two or three wheels, 2 brake horsepower or less, 50 cc or less, 30 mph — § 40-1-1(28). A moped operator carries any other Georgia driver's rights and duties — § 40-6-350. File within two years — O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 — and recover if less than 50% at fault — § 51-12-33.

_roden_faqs.question: Do you need a license to drive a moped in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-351 requires a driver's license, instruction permit or limited permit, and any class of them satisfies the statute — the section names no motorcycle endorsement. It also bars anyone under 15 from operating a moped, and a suspended license is not a valid one, so confirm your status first.

_roden_faqs.question: Do you have to register or insure a moped in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Georgia exempts mopeds from registration under O.C.G.A. § 40-2-20(b)(6), so that section requires no tag. It says nothing at all about insurance, and no verified Code section states whether a Georgia moped must be insured, so this page states no rule either way. Put that question to a Georgia attorney.

_roden_faqs.question: Is a helmet required on a moped in Georgia?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, for everyone. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-352 requires the operator and any passenger to wear protective headgear meeting the standards set by the Commissioner of Public Safety, with no age exemption, and an approved motorcycle helmet complies. The rule reaches an adult rider who would be exempt in other states, and it reaches the passenger riding behind you.

_roden_faqs.question: Can I still recover if I broke a moped rule when I was hit?
_roden_faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Georgia applies modified comparative fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33: you recover as long as you are less than 50% at fault, with your award reduced by your share. Riding without a helmet or a valid license gives the insurer an argument about percentages, answered with crash evidence and medical proof.

_roden_faqs.question: How long do I have to file a Georgia moped injury claim?
_roden_faqs.answer: Two years from the date of the crash, in most cases, under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Claims involving a government entity can carry shorter notice deadlines, so treat your window as shorter than you think. Evidence goes quickly in a moped case: the machine is repaired, intersection footage is overwritten, witnesses move on.
